\chapter{Eating, Drinking, Living --- the -er and -ir Verbs}
\label{ch:er-ir-verbs}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the singular forms of regular Spanish -er and -ir verbs to ask and answer what someone eats or drinks and where they live.}

Ask and answer a short exchange about eating, drinking, studying, and where someone lives, using the three singular regular verb patterns and only previously introduced words.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comer]{comer — \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} and the second verb family}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-comer}



\begin{quote}
Last chapter you learned the \textbf{-ar} verbs. Spanish has two more families — \textbf{-er} and \textbf{-ir} — and here's the good news: they're \textbf{almost the same}. Meet \textbf{comer} (\textquotedblleft{}to eat\textquotedblright{}), your first \textbf{-er} verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one soft tap: \emph{ko-\textbf{MER}}.
  \item The \emph{c} before \emph{o} is a hard \emph{k}: \emph{comer} = \emph{ko-MER}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{comer} comes from Latin \textbf{comedere}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to eat up\textquotedblright{}} — \textbf{com-} (intensifier, \textquotedblleft{}completely\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{edere}, \textquotedblleft{}to eat.\textquotedblright{} That \textbf{edere} is the twin of English \textbf{eat} (both from the same ancient root), and it feeds a small English family:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{edible} — fit to be eaten.
  \item \textbf{comestible} — a fancy word for food (straight from \emph{comedere}).
  \item English \textbf{eat} itself — the Germanic cousin of Latin \emph{edere}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -er present tense}]
The pattern is the \textbf{-ar} one with the \emph{a}'s swapped for \emph{e}'s. Drop \textbf{-er}, add:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{-ar was} & \textbf{\textbf{-er} is} & \textbf{\emph{comer} $\to$} \\
\midrule
yo & -o & \textbf{-o} & \textbf{como} (I eat) \\
tú & -as & \textbf{-es} & \textbf{comes} (you eat) \\
él/ella/usted & -a & \textbf{-e} & \textbf{come} (he/she eats) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the \textbf{yo} form is identical (\textbf{-o}), and \emph{tú}/\emph{él} just trade \emph{a} for \emph{e}: \emph{hablas/habla} $\to$ \emph{comes/come}. Those are the only three forms this lesson asks you to hold.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Watch the false friend:} \textbf{como} means \textquotedblleft{}I eat\textquotedblright{} \textbf{and} \textquotedblleft{}like/as\textquotedblright{} (\emph{como tú}, \textquotedblleft{}like you\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{and}, with an accent, \textbf{cómo} = \textquotedblleft{}how?\textquotedblright{}. Same four letters, three jobs — the accent and context sort them out.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}comer\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ko-MER}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}como, comes, come\textquotedblright{} — note the \emph{-o/-es/-e} endings
  \item \textquotedblleft{}comer\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}edible, comestible, eat\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{edere} family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{comer} from, and its English cousins? (\emph{comedere} $\leftarrow$ \emph{edere} — edible, eat.) What are the three singular \emph{-er} endings? (\emph{-o / -es / -e}.) How do they differ from \emph{-ar}? (The tú and usted vowels change from \emph{a} to \emph{e}.) Next: your first \textbf{-ir} verb, \emph{vivir}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vivir]{vivir — \textquotedblleft{}to live,\textquotedblright{} and the third family (that's barely new)}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-vivir}



\begin{quote}
The third and last verb family: \textbf{-ir}, and \textbf{vivir} (\textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{}) is your first. Here's the punchline — in the present tense, \textbf{-ir is almost identical to -er}. You've nearly finished learning the whole regular present.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{v-b} — Spanish \emph{v} = a soft \emph{b}: \emph{vivir} $\approx$ \emph{bee-BEER}.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one tap on the final \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vivir} comes from Latin \textbf{vīvere}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{}} — one of the most alive roots in English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{vivid} — \textquotedblleft{}full of life.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{survive} (\emph{super-vīvere}, \textquotedblleft{}to live beyond\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{revive} (\textquotedblleft{}live again\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{vivacious}, \textbf{convivial} (\textquotedblleft{}living together\textquotedblright{} — sociable), \textbf{viva!}, \textbf{vivarium}. (And \emph{vīta}, \textquotedblleft{}life,\textquotedblright{} gives \textbf{vital}, \textbf{vitamin}.)
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -ir present tense}]
Compare the three families, singular — this is the whole system:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{-ar (\emph{hablar})} & \textbf{-er (\emph{comer})} & \textbf{\textbf{-ir} (\emph{vivir})} \\
\midrule
yo & habl\textbf{o} & com\textbf{o} & \textbf{vivo} \\
tú & habl\textbf{as} & com\textbf{es} & \textbf{vives} \\
él/ella & habl\textbf{a} & com\textbf{e} & \textbf{vive} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look: \textbf{-er and -ir are identical in the singular} (\emph{-o / -es / -e}). They only part company in plural forms, which come later. For now, learning \emph{-ir} costs you almost nothing.

\textbf{Three families, one idea.} You can now build the three singular forms of a regular verb from any of the three families.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vivir\textquotedblright{} — \emph{bee-BEER}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vivo, vives, vive\textquotedblright{} — same endings as \emph{como, comes, come}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vivir\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}vivid, survive, revive\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{vīvere} family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{vivir} from, and two English cousins? (\emph{vīvere} — vivid, survive.) In the singular, how do \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} endings compare? (They're \textbf{identical}: \emph{-o / -es / -e}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I live.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vivo}.) Next: the drink verb, \emph{beber}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[beber]{beber — \textquotedblleft{}to drink,\textquotedblright{} and the pattern is yours}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-beber}



\begin{quote}
One more \textbf{-er} verb to make the pattern automatic — \textbf{beber}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink.\textquotedblright{} Pair it with \emph{comer} and you can talk about eating and drinking, the heart of any café or restaurant.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{v-b} — both \emph{b}'s are the soft Spanish \emph{b}: \emph{be-\textbf{BER}}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{beber} comes from Latin \textbf{bibere}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{}} — a thirsty little root that soaked into English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{beverage} — a drink (via Old French \emph{bevrage}, from \emph{bibere}).
  \item \textbf{imbibe} — to drink in (\emph{in-} + \emph{bibere}).
  \item \textbf{bibulous} — fond of drinking; \textbf{bib} — the cloth that catches drips; even \textbf{beer}'s cousins hover nearby.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no new grammar — that's the point}]
\emph{beber} is a regular \textbf{-er} verb, so it takes the endings you already own:

| yo | \textbf{bebo} | I drink |

| tú | \textbf{bebes} | you drink |

| él/ella/usted | \textbf{bebe} | he/she drinks / you (formal) drink |

Nothing new to learn — you're just \emph{reusing the machine}. With the word \emph{café} from the previous chapter, you can already say:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Bebo café.} — \textquotedblleft{}I drink coffee.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

One new verb, one known noun, one sentence you built yourself.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}beber\textquotedblright{} — \emph{be-BER}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bebo, bebes, bebe\textquotedblright{} — the familiar \emph{-o/-es/-e}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Bebo café\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}I drink coffee\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{beber} from, and its English cousins? (\emph{bibere} — beverage, imbibe.) Did \emph{beber} need any new endings? (No — it's a regular \emph{-er} verb.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I drink.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Bebo}.) Next: start \textbf{asking} — \emph{qué}, \textquotedblleft{}what?\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qué]{qué — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}, a new question word}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-que}



\begin{quote}
You already know the question word \emph{cómo}; now ask about a thing. The new question word is \textbf{qué}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} — and it puts to work two things from your writing chapter: the \textbf{accent} and the \textbf{¿ ?}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{k-hard} — \textbf{qu} is a plain hard \textbf{k} (the \emph{u} is silent): \emph{qué} = \emph{keh}.
  \item \texttt{accent-mark} — the \textbf{accent on \emph{é}} marks this as the \emph{question} word (recall the diacrítica: \emph{qué} = \textquotedblleft{}what?\textquotedblright{}; \emph{que} = \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}). Question words wear the accent.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{qué} comes from Latin \textbf{quid}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}} — the neuter of \emph{quis}, \textquotedblleft{}who.\textquotedblright{} It's a small function word with a few learned English descendants:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{quiddity} — the \textquotedblleft{}what-ness,\textquotedblright{} the essence of a thing.
  \item \textbf{quid pro quo} — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{what} for \emph{what},\textquotedblright{} this for that.
  \item the \emph{qu-} question family it heads in Spanish: \emph{qué, quién} (who), \emph{cuál} (which) — Latin's \emph{qu-} interrogatives, the same \emph{wh-} instinct as English (Latin \emph{qu-} and English \emph{wh-} are ancient cousins).
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: asking with a verb you know}]
Put \textbf{qué} in front of a verb, wrap it in \textbf{¿ ?}, and you have a real question:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{¿Qué comes?} — \textquotedblleft{}What are you eating? / What do you eat?\textquotedblright{} \textbf{¿Qué bebes?} — \textquotedblleft{}What are you drinking?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Remember the opening \textbf{¿} (from the writing lesson) warns the reader a question is coming; the accent on \emph{qué} marks it as the question word. Answer with the verb you already conjugate and a noun you already know: \emph{Bebo café.} (\textquotedblleft{}I drink coffee.\textquotedblright{})
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}qué\textquotedblright{} — \emph{keh}, silent \emph{u}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Qué comes?\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}¿Qué bebes?\textquotedblright{} — ask with verbs you know
  \item \textquotedblleft{}qué\textquotedblright{} vs \textquotedblleft{}que\textquotedblright{} — the accent marks the \emph{question}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{qué} from? (\emph{quid} — quiddity, quid pro quo.) Why does \emph{qué} carry an accent? (It's the \emph{question} word; \emph{que} without = \textquotedblleft{}that.\textquotedblright{}) Ask \textquotedblleft{}what are you eating?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{¿Qué comes?}) Next: asking \textbf{where} — \emph{dónde}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dónde]{dónde — \textquotedblleft{}where?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-donde}



\begin{quote}
One more question word, and one more real question you can build: \textbf{dónde}, \textquotedblleft{}where?\textquotedblright{} Pair it with \emph{vivir} and you can ask the single most common getting-to-know-you question: \emph{where do you live?}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{d-soft} — the middle \emph{d} is soft, near the \emph{th} of \emph{this}: \emph{DON-deh}.
  \item \texttt{accent-mark} — like \emph{qué}, the \textbf{accent on \emph{ó}} marks the question word (\emph{dónde} = \textquotedblleft{}where?\textquotedblright{}; \emph{donde} without = \textquotedblleft{}where,\textquotedblright{} a relative — \textquotedblleft{}the place \emph{where}\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dónde} comes from Latin \textbf{de unde}, literally \emph{\textquotedblleft{}from whence.\textquotedblright{}} \emph{unde} meant \textquotedblleft{}from where,\textquotedblright{} and Spanish glued \emph{de} onto the front and wore the pair down to \emph{dónde}. (English once had the matching set \emph{whence / where / whither} — \textquotedblleft{}from where / at where / to where\textquotedblright{}; Spanish keeps that flavour in \emph{de dónde} \textquotedblleft{}from where\textquotedblright{}, \emph{dónde} \textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}, \emph{adónde} \textquotedblleft{}to where\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: your first getting-to-know-you questions}]
Two question words + verbs you own = real conversation:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{¿Dónde vives?} — \textquotedblleft{}Where do you live?\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{Vivo en Madrid.} \textbf{¿Dónde trabajas?} — \textquotedblleft{}Where do you work?\textquotedblright{} \textbf{¿Qué estudias?} — \textquotedblleft{}What do you study?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Notice the little \textbf{en} (\textquotedblleft{}in,\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{in}) in the answer — the first preposition, slipping in exactly where you need it. You're now trading real questions and answers, not fixed phrases.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dónde\textquotedblright{} — \emph{DON-deh}, soft \emph{d}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Dónde vives?\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}Where do you live?\textquotedblright{}
  \item answer — \textquotedblleft{}Vivo en …\textquotedblright{} with your city
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin phrase is \emph{dónde} from, and what did it mean? (\emph{De unde} — \textquotedblleft{}from whence.\textquotedblright{}) Why the accent? (It marks the \emph{question} word.) Ask \textquotedblleft{}where do you live?\textquotedblright{} and answer it. (\emph{¿Dónde vives? — Vivo en …}) Next: put the questions and verbs together in practice.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — asking real questions}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-practice}



\begin{quote}
You now have all three verb families \textbf{and} two question words. This is where it becomes a conversation: you can \textbf{ask} and \textbf{answer}, not just recite. Drill until the questions come without thinking.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three singular patterns}]
Conjugate \emph{yo $\to$ tú $\to$ él/ella} — feel how little differs:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{-ar} \emph{hablar}: hablo · hablas · habla
  \item \textbf{-er} \emph{comer}: como · comes · come
  \item \textbf{-ir} \emph{vivir}: vivo · vives · vive
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Endings:} \emph{-ar} $\to$ -o/-as/-a; \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} $\to$ \textbf{-o/-es/-e} in these three singular forms. The plural forms can wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange — use only what you know}
\begin{quote}
— ¿\textbf{Dónde vives}? — \textbf{Vivo} en Sevilla. ¿Y tú? — \textbf{Vivo} en México. — ¿\textbf{Qué estudias}? — \textbf{Estudio} español. ¿\textbf{Qué bebes}? — \textbf{Bebo} café.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{comer / beber} (-er), \textbf{vivir} (-ir) — the two remaining verb families; singular endings \textbf{-o / -es / -e}.
  \item \textbf{qué} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{quid}) and \textbf{dónde} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{de unde}) — your first question words, each wearing the \textbf{accent} and opening with \textbf{¿}.
  \item \textbf{Real questions}: \emph{¿Qué comes? ¿Dónde vives? ¿Dónde trabajas?} — and the first preposition, \textbf{en} (\textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}), in the answers.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item conjugate all three families, yo/tú/él, back to back
  \item ask a friend where they live and what they drink; answer both
  \item ask what they study; answer \textquotedblleft{}Estudio español\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}¿Dónde vives? — Vivo en … ¿Y tú?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the singular endings for \emph{-er/-ir} verbs? (\emph{-o / -es / -e}.) Give the \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms of \emph{comer, vivir, beber}. (\emph{Como, vivo, bebo}.) Ask \textquotedblleft{}what do you study?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}where do you live?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{¿Qué estudias? ¿Dónde vives?}) You can now hold a simple back-and-forth — this book is fully in sentence territory. Next: \textbf{numbers} (uno, dos, tres) and telling someone your age and phone.
\end{tcolorbox}
